paragraphs.text: Meta Superintelligence Lab released Muse Ember on November 9, 2026, describing it as the lab's lightest and most cost-efficient model so far. Meta built it for repetitive work inside AI agents, such as tool calls, coding subtasks, routing requests, extracting data and parsing long documents, according to TechCrunch.

Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, The Next Web reported. It is available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, Meta's coding tool. As with earlier Muse releases, the model weights remain private.

Meta frames the release around cost per task rather than price per token, using the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an independent composite benchmark. On that index, Ember scores 36 at its highest reasoning setting, the same as Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 at its highest setting, while OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna scores 28, according to The Next Web.

By Meta's own figures, Ember costs about $0.14 per index task, compared with $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. That puts Ember level with Haiku at roughly a third of the cost. Meta also reported that Ember scored 37.8 percent on AutomationBench, a test of full business workflows, against 20.2 percent for Luna and 13.9 percent for Haiku.

The model does not lead everywhere. On FrontierCode 2.0, which measures whether maintainers would merge a model's code changes, Haiku scored 34.9 percent and Ember 27.2 percent. Some of the results Meta published, including its Personal Superintelligence Index, come from internal tests.
A worker for a larger planner

Meta positions Ember as a partner to Muse Wonder, its frontier model released in October. In Meta's example, a larger model writes the rules for handling customer support cases and Ember applies them across tens of thousands of cases. Ember accepts text, images and audio, so an agent can read screenshots, charts and scanned documents without a separate model, TechCrunch reported.

Ember is the fourth Muse model, after Spark in April, its open source twin Glimmer in August and Wonder in October. The Next Web reported that Ember is the first model Meta trained using the larger Muse Wonder Full, that Meta tested it against its safety framework and found it below the high-risk thresholds in every category, and that Meta says even more efficient models are in training.

Small models matter because agents call them constantly. A product that runs thousands of tool calls or document checks a day pays for every one, so a model that matches a rival's score at a lower cost per task can change which provider a developer picks. The comparison rests partly on Meta's own cost figures, and the coding result shows the trade-offs are not uniform.
Watch whether independent testers confirm Meta's cost per task figures, and whether Anthropic and OpenAI respond with price changes for Haiku and Luna.
